text.title_en: The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra “The Basket’s Display”
text.canon: Degé Kangyur, vol. 51 (mdo sde, pa), folios 200.a–247.b
text.translators: Peter Alan Roberts with Tulku Yeshi (English); Jinamitra, Dānaśīla and Yeshé Dé (Tibetan)
text.publisher: 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha

notes.text: A sūtra told as narratives within narratives about Avalokiteśvara’s activity in many realms, including the realms within the pores of his skin. It closes on how rare his mantra is: on the Buddha’s instruction, the bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin obtains it from a man in Vārāṇasī who has broken his monastic vows.
The mantra itself appears twice: Avalokiteśvara gives it to the Tathāgata Padmottama (¶2.57), and later it is given to Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, who receives it with palms joined (¶2.76).
The sūtra praises the merit of repeating the mantra as beyond calculation. That is the text’s own teaching, given here as what it says, not as a promised effect of reciting.

The sūtra explains neither the mantra as a whole nor its individual syllables. Syllable-by-syllable explanations became widespread later in Tibetan Buddhism, and the meaning has been understood in various ways.

Reading padme as a locative gives the familiar “jewel in the lotus.” The translator argues that padme is a Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit vocative, making Maṇipadma (“Jewel Lotus”) a name by which Avalokiteśvara is invoked. This is the translator’s argument, not a settled consensus.
